note: Season 0 rounds. Lock is always release minus 48 hours, except behavioral series (wikipedia, google_trends), which lock before the measured week begins because their outcome data publishes daily. Times are UTC. release_estimated=true means the pollster does not preannounce an exact time; if a wave slips, the round resolves on the next published wave. Nothing here is written automatically: tools/generate_rounds.py drafts candidates into questions/candidates/ and never touches this file, and every round below is frozen by the commit that added it. The weekly families (wiki_top10, the Trends brand basket) are rolled forward from a reviewed round rather than rewritten each week -- the generator refuses to emit one whose wording it cannot rebuild from the reviewed original, so a rolled-forward week asks the question a human approved and not a paraphrase of it.

rounds.question: Economist/YouGov weekly tracker: Donald Trump's job approval among US registered voters, broken into the survey's own sixteen crosstab cells, for September 2026. Forecast the percentage approving in each subgroup, averaged over the four weekly waves dated in September 2026 (expected 2026-09-07, 09-14, 09-21 and 09-28). These are measured cells of one survey, not a model's subgroup estimates: they move with the national mood and they also move apart, and the whole profile is scored.
rounds.resolve: for each of the sixteen cells, the mean of that cell's approve percentage over the four weekly Economist/YouGov waves dated in September 2026, read from the tracker workbook. If September carries five waves the last four dated in September are averaged, so the target is always a four-wave mean; if it carries fewer than four the round does not resolve rather than averaging three. The month's point is dated by the last of those four waves, which is why the lock sits on that wave's own date: one day later and the answer would fall inside the strictly-pre-lock history its own persistence null is built from.

rounds.resolve: the September 2026 row of the frbny-sce-data.xlsx vintage archived under sources/sce/ on release day; the release date is preannounced on the NY Fed economic-indicators calendar, the hour (11:00 ET) is convention, hence release_estimated

rounds.question: Google Trends, United States: the share of weekly search interest taken by each of Tesla, iPhone, Samsung, Netflix and Disney for the week Sun Oct 11 - Sat Oct 17, 2026. All five are measured in one comparison request, so their weekly indices sit on a single shared scale; forecast each brand's percentage of the five-brand total. The five shares add to 100.
rounds.unit: percent of the five-brand basket (the five add to 100)
rounds.resolve: the first archived five-query comparison snapshot (US, web search, trailing 12-month window) carrying the completed week ending 2026-10-17; each brand's value divided by the sum over the five, in percent

rounds.question: The ordered top-10 articles on the English Wikipedia by pageviews for the week Mon Oct 12 - Sun Oct 18, 2026. The seven daily top-1000 lists published by Wikimedia are summed per article and ranked; Main_Page and every non-article namespace (Special:, Wikipedia:, Portal:, Help:, File:, Template:, Category:, Draft:, User:, Talk: and their _talk: variants) are excluded. Give the ten article titles in order, rank 1 first.
rounds.resolve: Wikimedia daily top endpoint (top/en.wikipedia/all-access), the week's seven archived daily lists summed per article, exclusion rule main_page_and_namespaces_v1 applied, top 10 by weekly total, ties broken by title ascending. An article absent from a day's top-1000 contributes zero for that day.
rounds.unit: ordered list of 10 en.wikipedia article titles, canonical underscore form, rank 1 first

rounds.question: Harvard CAPS/Harris Poll, produced jointly by Harvard's Center for American Political Studies and The Harris Poll as a roughly monthly online survey of US registered voters: percent who approve (strongly or somewhat) of the job Donald J. Trump is doing as President, in the NEXT wave published after this round's lock. Harvard-Harris announces no calendar and skips some months, so the target is defined by publication order, not by a date: whatever wave's topline appears first after the lock is the one scored, whenever it lands. Recent waves printed 42, 43, 42 percent approve.
rounds.resolve: the M3ALT strongly/somewhat approve net in the first topline PDF archived under sources/hhpoll/ whose production stamp is after lock_at; the series is dated by publication stamp, so this is the first series point after the frozen pre-lock history
